concept_note.title: Vector Databases: Indexes, Hybrid Search, and Production Patterns
concept_note.summary: HNSW graphs, IVF clusters, hybrid search, and metadata filtering turn embeddings into production-grade retrieval systems.
learning_goals: Understand HNSW and IVF index structures
Understand metadata filtering and pre/post filtering trade-offs
Design a retrieval pipeline for RAG
concept_note.long_intro: You know a vector database stores embeddings and answers nearest-neighbour queries. This lesson goes deep on the three techniques that make them production-grade. HNSW builds a navigable graph to find near-neighbours in sublinear time. IVF clusters vectors and searches only nearby clusters. Hybrid search combines vector similarity with traditional keyword search (BM25) for the best of both worlds. Metadata filtering lets you restrict search to a subset ('only documents from 2023'). Together these give the flexibility and speed that production search and RAG systems need.

deep_explanation.heading: HNSW: graph-based navigation
deep_explanation.body: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph. The top layer has a few well-connected nodes; the bottom layer has all nodes, each connected to its nearest neighbours. Search starts at the top, greedily moves to the nearest node, drops down a layer, and repeats. At the bottom layer, it explores a small neighbourhood and returns the closest points found. The key insight: at each layer, we only visit a handful of nodes, so total comparisons are O(log n) instead of O(n). This is why HNSW is fast.
deep_explanation.code:
# HNSW search (conceptual)
# Layer 3 (sparse):     start here, move greedily to nearest
# Layer 2:              drop down, move greedily again
# Layer 1:              drop down, move to local region
# Layer 0 (all nodes):  explore neighbourhood, return top-K

# Result: ~O(log n) comparisons per query

print("HNSW: greedy descent through layers, then local search")

deep_explanation.heading: IVF: inverted file index
deep_explanation.body: IVF (Inverted File) partitions the vector space into K clusters using k-means. Each cluster has a centroid. When a query arrives, the system finds the n_probe nearest centroids and searches only the vectors in those clusters. This reduces the search to a fraction of the total. The trade-off: if the nearest vector is in a cluster whose centroid is far from the query, it will be missed. Tuning n_probe adjusts the recall/speed trade-off.
deep_explanation.code:
# IVF search (conceptual)
#
# Training: k-means on the corpus, get K centroids
# Indexing: assign each vector to its nearest centroid
# Query:
#   1. Find the n_probe nearest centroids to the query
#   2. Search only vectors in those clusters
#   3. Return top-K

K = 100          # number of clusters
n_probe = 5      # search 5 nearest clusters per query

print(f"IVF: {K} clusters, searching {n_probe} per query")

deep_explanation.heading: Hybrid search: vector + keyword
deep_explanation.body: Vector search finds semantic matches but can miss exact terms. Keyword search (BM25) finds exact terms but misses paraphrases. Hybrid search combines both. Typically, you run both searches and merge the ranked results with a weighting scheme (Reciprocal Rank Fusion is common). Many production systems use hybrid search as their default, especially for technical or legal content where exact terms matter.

deep_explanation.heading: Metadata filtering: pre and post
deep_explanation.body: Metadata filters restrict which vectors can match. Two approaches: pre-filtering (filter first, then search within the filtered set) and post-filtering (search first, filter after). Pre-filtering is more accurate but can be slow if the filter is selective. Post-filtering is fast but might return too few results after filtering. Production systems use hybrid strategies: if the filter is broad, pre-filter; if narrow, post-filter and re-query.
deep_explanation.code:
# Metadata filter examples
documents = [
    {"id": "doc1", "year": 2023, "category": "ml",    "vector": [0.9, 0.1]},
    {"id": "doc2", "year": 2022, "category": "ml",    "vector": [0.8, 0.2]},
    {"id": "doc3", "year": 2023, "category": "finance", "vector": [0.1, 0.9]},
]

# Pre-filter: only 2023 documents
filtered = [d for d in documents if d["year"] == 2023]
print(f"Pre-filter kept {len(filtered)} of {len(documents)}")

# Now search within filtered set
query = [0.85, 0.15]
def cosine(a, b):
    import math
    d = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    return d / (math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in b)))

results = sorted(filtered, key=lambda d: -cosine(query, d["vector"]))
print("Top result:", results[0]["id"])

concept_note.formal_definition: Vector indexes fall into two broad categories: graph-based (HNSW) and cluster-based (IVF). HNSW provides excellent recall and speed at the cost of memory; IVF is more memory-efficient and scales better to enormous corpora. Hybrid search combines dense vector similarity with sparse keyword relevance (BM25) via rank fusion. Metadata filtering supports pre-filter (index-time constraints) or post-filter (rerank after ANN search). Production systems tune index parameters (M, efConstruction, n_probe) to balance recall, latency, and memory.

code_example.universal_explanation: The hybrid search runs a vector search (semantic similarity) and a keyword search (exact term match) in parallel, then combines results with reciprocal rank fusion. Documents that rank high on both get boosted. This is the standard approach in production RAG systems.

common_mistakes: Using one index type for everything: HNSW is best for high-recall, low-latency at moderate scale; IVF is better for huge corpora on constrained memory.
Forgetting to re-embed when the query model changes: if you update your embedding model, all indexed vectors must be regenerated.
Skipping metadata filtering when it is needed: many enterprise searches must be scoped to a tenant, date range, or category.
Ignoring recall metrics: ANN is approximate. Measure recall@k on a validation set to know how often the true nearest neighbour is actually returned.
concept_note.real_world_usage: Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, and pgvector all implement HNSW and/or IVF. Production search systems at Google, Meta, and Spotify use hybrid search with metadata filtering. RAG pipelines for enterprise AI usually combine: (1) chunk the documents, (2) embed with a strong model, (3) index in a vector database, (4) at query time, run hybrid search, (5) rerank with a cross-encoder, (6) pass top-K to the LLM.
key_takeaways: HNSW uses a multi-layer graph to find near-neighbours in sublinear time.
IVF clusters vectors and searches only nearby clusters.
Hybrid search combines vector similarity with BM25 keyword matching.
Metadata filtering restricts search and can be pre- or post-filter.
Production retrieval combines all these techniques in a pipeline.

activity.sentence: HNSW stands for Hierarchical Navigable Small ___.

activity.question: IVF searches only a subset of clusters per query. What is the trade-off?
choices: It is always faster with no downside
It can miss vectors whose cluster centroid is far from the query
It uses more memory than HNSW
activity.reveal: IVF only searches clusters whose centroids are close to the query. If the true nearest vector is in a cluster with a distant centroid, it will be missed. Tuning n_probe adjusts the speed/recall trade-off.

activity.question: You are searching a legal database and need to find documents that mention an exact case name AND are semantically related to a query. Which approach?
activity.reveal: Hybrid search combines semantic similarity (for the query) with keyword matching (for the exact case name). Pure vector search might miss the exact term; pure keyword search might miss paraphrases.

activity.code:
# Metadata filter example
docs = [
    {"id": "d1", "year": 2023, "vector": [0.9, 0.1]},
    {"id": "d2", "year": 2024, "vector": [0.85, 0.15]},
]

# Want only 2023 documents, but filter was applied AFTER search
query = [0.88, 0.12]
results = sorted(docs, key=lambda d: -cosine(query, d["vector"]))
filtered = [d for d in results if d["year"] == 2023]
# Too few results may remain after filtering
activity.explanation: Post-filtering (search first, then filter) can leave too few results if the filter is selective. If only 5% of documents are from 2023, searching top-10 gives ~0.5 expected matches. Pre-filtering (filter first, then search) guarantees enough results, though it is more expensive on large indexes.

activity.prompt: In your own words, explain the difference between HNSW and IVF indexes.
activity.rubric: Should mention HNSW is graph-based (multi-layer navigable graph), IVF is cluster-based (partitioned by k-means centroids). Both are approximate; HNSW is faster and more accurate at cost of memory, IVF is more memory-efficient.

test.sentence: IVF uses k-means to partition vectors into clusters; search happens only in the nearest ___ clusters.

test.question: Which combination is best for a search system where both exact terms and paraphrase matter?
choices: Hybrid search combining both via rank fusion
test.reveal: Hybrid search runs both and fuses the results, so it captures exact term matches and semantic similarity.

test.question: You have a filter that keeps only 1% of documents. Which filtering strategy is safest?
choices: Pre-filter (filter first, then search within the filtered set)
test.reveal: Post-filtering with a selective filter leaves too few results. Pre-filtering guarantees you search only within the matching subset, so you get enough results from the ANN index.

items: Embed all documents and store vectors plus metadata
Build an HNSW or IVF index over the vectors
At query time, embed the query and search the index for near-neighbours
Apply metadata filters (pre or post depending on selectivity)
Fuse with keyword search results if using hybrid retrieval

test.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain what reciprocal rank fusion does in hybrid search.
test.rubric: Should mention that it combines ranked lists from multiple retrieval methods (vector and keyword) by summing 1/(k+rank) for each document, so documents ranked high on multiple lists get boosted.
